content.text:
Now I'll analyze the data before writing the candidates file. Key findings from the brief:

- **R1 (screening) and R3 (mass) and R4 (thickness) are never binding** in this design space — even thick copper plates pass R1/R4 easily, and thin graphite plates pass R3 by a huge margin.
- **R2 (FE hotspot) is the only real constraint**, and remarkably it's **flat with thickness**: pure graphite gives 325 K at 10, 20, and 30 mm; pure aluminium gives 324 K at 10–30 mm; pure copper gives 322 K at 10–30 mm. This means thickness beyond some (unknown, but ≤10 mm) saturation point buys nothing — the hotspot is set almost entirely by the face material's conductivity, not by having more of it.
- Corroborating evidence: adding just **2 mm of copper cladding** onto a 10 mm aluminium base already achieves nearly all of copper's benefit (324→323 K), and adding more copper (3 mm, 5 mm) gives **zero further improvement** (323 K flat). So the spreading effect saturates within a couple of millimetres of the heated face.

This strongly suggests graphite (lightest usable conductor, k=150, ρ=1800) can likely be used far thinner than 10 mm while staying near the 325 K plateau, since we're never shown data proving 10 mm is *required* — only that 10-30mm range change made no difference. I'll submit a graduated sweep of pure-graphite thicknesses down toward the aggressive end, plus a few thin copper-faced hybrids as insurance that use copper's superior local spreading at minimal added mass, bridging the risk gap.

10 candidate(s) submitted in one call; none evaluated in this session.

| candidate | design | rationale |
| --- | --- | --- |
| c-0000 | 10 mm graphite | Exact match to the prior campaign-1 point (10 mm graphite), which Core scored PASS on all four requirements: screen 403 K (<=420), FE hotspot 325 K (<=340, 15 K margin), mass 18 kg/m^2 (<=100), thickness 1 cm (<=4 cm). This is the lightest design in the prior record's PASS set (18 kg/m^2, versus 27 for 10 mm aluminium and 89.6 for 10 mm copper), so it is my safe anchor: I am highly confident it meets every requirement because it is directly validated, not extrapolated. |
| c-0001 | 8 mm graphite | Graphite's FE hotspot was identical (325 K) at 10, 20, and 30 mm in the prior sweep, showing R2 is flat/insensitive to added thickness in that range, i.e. the plate is already past whatever thickness the spreading effect needs to saturate. Trimming 2 mm from the validated 10 mm point is a small step back toward that saturation threshold, so I believe 325 K (or very close to it) still holds, giving mass 14.4 kg/m^2 - 20% lighter than the prior record with low incremental risk. |
| c-0002 | 6 mm graphite | Continuing the same reasoning: graphite's hotspot did not move at all between 10-30 mm, so the true saturation thickness is at or below 10 mm. 6 mm is a moderate extrapolation below the validated point but still well above the 2 mm scale at which copper cladding (see the 2/3/5 mm copper-on-aluminium prior points, all identical 323 K) demonstrated that local spreading saturates. Mass 10.8 kg/m^2, thickness 6 mm, screening estimate ~400 K (formula ~399+60*t/k, negligible thickness sensitivity) - comfortably inside every limit. |
| c-0003 | 5 mm graphite | Halfway between the validated 10 mm point and the 2 mm scale shown sufficient for copper cladding to fully realize its spreading benefit. Mass 9.0 kg/m^2. I believe the FE hotspot stays close to the 325 K plateau given the flatness evidence, leaving ample margin to the 340 K limit; mass/thickness limits are not remotely challenged (9 kg/m^2 vs 100, 5 mm vs 40 mm). |
| c-0004 | 4 mm graphite | More aggressive thinning, motivated directly by the cladding evidence: 2 mm of copper on top of an already-saturated 10 mm aluminium base captured copper's full incremental spreading benefit, and adding a 3rd and 5th mm of copper added nothing further (323 K flat). That implies a couple of millimetres of high/mid-conductivity material at the heated face is enough to establish the lateral spreading path for this geometry. At 4 mm, graphite mass is only 7.2 kg/m^2. Confidence is moderate rather than high since this has no direct prior data point, but the physical reasoning and the large 15 K margin seen at 10 mm give me reasonable belief it still clears 340 K. |
| c-0005 | 3 mm graphite | My boldest pure-material bet: 3 mm approaches the ~2 mm scale at which copper cladding was shown to already saturate its spreading benefit. Graphite has lower conductivity than copper (150 vs 400 W/mK) so its own saturation thickness could plausibly be somewhat larger, but even a partial shortfall from the 325 K plateau has 15 K of headroom to spend before hitting the 340 K limit. Mass is 5.4 kg/m^2, roughly a third of the prior record's lightest PASS design. I include this as an aggressive, still-reasoned candidate rather than a safe one. |
| c-0006 | 2 mm graphite | The lightest candidate in this set: mass 3.6 kg/m^2, thickness 2 mm, directly mirroring the 2 mm depth at which copper cladding in the prior sweep already achieved its full spreading benefit atop a saturated base. This is a genuine extrapolation with the least supporting margin of the set, but I include it because the flat R2 trend from 10-30 mm and the fast saturation shown by the copper-cladding data both point toward spreading resistance being dominated by a small near-surface thickness, not by having 10 mm of material. Screening and mass/thickness limits are not remotely at risk here. |
| c-0007 | 1 mm copper + 2 mm graphite | Hybrid insurance candidate pairing a thin, high-conductivity copper face (for local spreading right at the heated face, where the prior sweep shows conductivity matters most) with a thin graphite backing to keep mass low. Total thickness 3 mm, mass 8.96 + 3.6 = 12.56 kg/m^2 - still well under the prior record's lightest PASS design (18 kg/m^2) but with a stronger physical case for adequate near-surface spreading than the pure 3 mm graphite option above, since copper's higher conductivity should reach the spreading plateau at a shallower depth than graphite would need alone. |
| c-0008 | 1 mm copper + 3 mm graphite | Same copper-face/graphite-backing logic as the previous candidate but with a slightly thicker graphite backing (3 mm) for extra bulk-conduction margin, total thickness 4 mm, mass 8.96 + 5.4 = 14.36 kg/m^2. Positioned as a moderate-confidence fallback between the pure thin-graphite bets and the higher-confidence copper-clad option below, still well under the prior record's lightest validated mass of 18 kg/m^2. |
| c-0009 | 2 mm copper + 3 mm graphite | Highest-confidence hybrid: 2 mm of copper directly replicates the exact cladding depth shown in the prior sweep to fully capture copper's spreading benefit (2, 3, and 5 mm copper claddings on aluminium all gave the same 323 K), backed by 3 mm of graphite for bulk conduction margin. Total thickness 5 mm, mass 17.92 + 5.4 = 23.32 kg/m^2. This is heavier than the pure-graphite anchor (18 kg/m^2) but included as the strongest-evidenced insurance point for the low-thickness regime, and is still far lighter than every other prior PASS design besides plain 10 mm graphite (27-89.6 kg/m^2 for the rest). |

content.text:
## Final report

**Prior record's lightest PASS design:** 10 mm graphite, 18 kg/m² (screen 403 K, FE hotspot 325 K, mass 18 kg/m², thickness 1 cm — all pass).

**Key finding from the brief that shaped my whole approach:** the FE hotspot (R2, the only requirement with any real margin pressure) was essentially *flat with thickness* for every pure material tested — graphite held at 325 K across 10/20/30 mm, aluminium at 324 K, copper at 322 K. Meanwhile, layering just 2 mm of copper onto a 10 mm aluminium base already captured copper's full spreading benefit (324→323 K), and adding a 3rd or 5th mm of copper added nothing further. Together these say the hotspot is governed by a near-surface spreading effect that saturates within a few millimetres, not by the total plate thickness — so 10 mm is very likely far more material than is needed, and R1/R3/R4 have so much slack (even at low thickness) that they're never at risk.

**Submitted set (10 candidates, graphite as the primary material since it's the lightest usable conductor: k=150 W/mK, ρ=1800 kg/m³, clearly better mass-for-performance than aluminium or copper):**

| candidate | design | mass (kg/m²) |
|---|---|---|
